Curiously enough, I thought this was somewhat at odds with the agreement twitter signed with the US Library of Congress regarding a permanent archive of world communications (AKA tweets). Looking over the whitepaper (PDF Link) posted 3 years after the original agreement it seems twitter has been working on this data monetization for years and made sure that the LoC deal wouldn't jeopardize any later data selling programs.

The Library of Congress Agreement with Twitter

  • The Library could make available any portion of the collection six months after it was originally posted on Twitter to “bona fide” researchers.

  • A researcher must sign a “notification” prohibiting commercial use and redistribution of the collection.

  • The Library cannot provide a substantial portion of the collection on its web site

    in a form that can be easily downloaded.

If you are a commercial venture and want access to recent (< 6 month old) data, you'll have to pay. Oddly enough, if you're a research institution working on a project that would benefit from twitter information, you can ignore the LoC program entirely and apply for a "#DataGrant" that seems to use the exact backend developed by Gnip for the LoC agreement.

Here's an interesting bit regarding the total size of the tweet corpus as of 2012:

As of December 1, 2012, the Library has received more than 150 billion additional tweets and corresponding metadata, for a total including the 2006 - 2010 archive of approximately 170 billion tweets totaling 133.2 terabytes for two compressed copies.
